title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
intro: End-to-end tests verify that your application works as a complete system from the user's point of view. In this lesson, you'll use Playwright to test a React frontend together with a Spring Boot backend, and learn how to keep E2E tests reliable enough for CI.
body:
## What an end-to-end test proves

An end-to-end (E2E) test exercises your application through the same kind of interface a real user uses. Instead of testing one React component or one Spring service in isolation, an E2E test can start at the browser and travel through the whole application stack.

For your task manager, a single test might do this:

~~~text
Browser
  ↓
React application
  ↓
HTTP request
  ↓
Spring Boot controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Repository
  ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

The test can then verify that the resulting task appears in the browser.

This gives you a different kind of confidence from unit and integration tests. A unit test can prove that a service behaves correctly. A frontend test can prove that a component renders correctly. An E2E test can prove that the important pieces work together in a realistic user flow.

That confidence comes at a cost. E2E tests are slower, more complex, and usually more sensitive to environment problems than unit tests. Starting a browser, running the frontend and backend, making HTTP requests, and interacting with a real database all take time.

That is why the testing pyramid contains relatively few E2E tests. You want enough to protect your most important workflows, but you do not want every small behaviour to require a full browser test.

## Why Playwright

[Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) is a browser automation and end-to-end testing framework. It can control browsers, navigate to pages, interact with forms, and make assertions about what users can see.

It supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, which makes it useful when browser compatibility matters.

A Playwright test can look surprisingly close to a manual test:

~~~ts
await page.goto('http://localhost:5173');
await page.getByLabel('Title').fill('Prepare report');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }).click();
await expect(page.getByText('Prepare report')).toBeVisible();
~~~

This is one of the biggest advantages of E2E tests: the test describes an actual user journey.

## Installing Playwright

In your Vite + React + TypeScript frontend project, install Playwright using its project setup command.

~~~shell
npm init playwright@latest
~~~

The setup asks questions about the test directory, TypeScript, GitHub Actions, and whether browsers should be installed.

A typical project will end up with a Playwright configuration and a test directory. A test might look like this:

~~~ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can add a task', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://localhost:5173');

  await page.getByLabel('Title').fill('Prepare report');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Prepare report')).toBeVisible();
});
~~~

The exact URL should normally come from your Playwright configuration rather than being repeated throughout every test.

## Locators describe the user interface

Playwright provides several ways to locate elements. Prefer locators that represent how a user interacts with the application.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Brittle selector", "lang": "ts", "code": "await page.click(\n  'div.form > div:nth-child(3) > button'\n);", "note": "Breaks on any markup change."}, "right": {"title": "User-facing locator", "lang": "ts", "code": "await page\n  .getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' })\n  .click();", "note": "Survives refactors and checks accessibility for free."}}
~~~

For form controls, labels are particularly useful:

~~~ts
await page.getByLabel('Title').fill('Prepare report');
~~~

For buttons, roles and accessible names are usually a strong choice:

~~~ts
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }).click();
~~~

You can also locate headings, links, checkboxes, list items, and other semantic elements by role.

This approach has an important side effect: it encourages you to build accessible interfaces. If an input has a proper label and a button has a meaningful accessible name, both users and automated tests can identify them reliably.

Avoid building your entire E2E suite around CSS selectors such as `.button.primary` or deeply nested selectors. Styling changes should not break a test that is still valid from the user's perspective.

## Auto-waiting

One of Playwright's most useful features is automatic waiting.

Suppose clicking a button starts an API request. The task might not appear immediately. A naive browser automation script might insert a fixed delay:

~~~ts
await page.waitForTimeout(2000);
~~~

This is usually a poor solution. If the server responds in 100 milliseconds, you wasted almost two seconds. If the server takes three seconds, the test can still fail.

Playwright's locators and assertions can wait for the expected condition.

~~~ts
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }).click();
await expect(page.getByText('Prepare report')).toBeVisible();
~~~

The assertion waits for the element to become visible within the configured timeout.

Similarly, you can check text directly:

~~~ts
await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Task added');
~~~

This is much more stable than guessing how long an operation will take.

## Testing a complete login flow

Imagine your task manager requires authentication. An important E2E test might start with a login page.

~~~diagram
{"type": "sequence", "title": "One E2E test, end to end", "actors": ["Playwright", "Browser", "App (React + API + DB)"], "steps": [{"from": "Playwright", "to": "Browser", "label": "goto('/login')"}, {"from": "Playwright", "to": "Browser", "label": "fill email + password · click Log in"}, {"from": "Browser", "to": "App (React + API + DB)", "label": "POST /api/auth/login"}, {"from": "App (React + API + DB)", "to": "Browser", "label": "token → /dashboard", "dashed": true}, {"note": "auto-waits for the heading", "over": "Playwright"}, {"from": "Playwright", "to": "Browser", "label": "expect(heading 'Dashboard').toBeVisible()"}]}
~~~

The test could enter credentials, submit the form, and verify that the authenticated application appears:

~~~ts
await page.goto('/login');

await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('anna@example.com');
await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('correct-password');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();

await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Tasks' })).toBeVisible();
~~~

This can exercise several layers at once:

- React renders the login form.
- The browser sends the request.
- Spring Boot receives the request.
- Authentication validates the credentials.
- The backend creates or returns the authentication state.
- The frontend handles the response.
- The authenticated task page becomes visible.

That is much more valuable than testing only that a Login button exists.

## Testing login and task creation together

The most useful E2E tests often represent critical business workflows.

For the task manager, one valuable scenario could be:

~~~text
Open application
    ↓
Log in
    ↓
Open task page
    ↓
Enter task title
    ↓
Submit task
    ↓
Backend stores task
    ↓
Task appears in browser
~~~

A Playwright test might contain:

~~~ts
await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('anna@example.com');
await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('correct-password');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();

await page.getByLabel('Task title').fill('Prepare quarterly report');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }).click();

await expect(
  page.getByRole('listitem', { name: 'Prepare quarterly report' })
).toBeVisible();
~~~

Notice that the test does not need to know which React component owns the form or which Spring service creates the task. It cares about the user-visible workflow.

## Test data and database reset

E2E tests become unreliable when they depend on data left behind by previous tests.

Imagine one test creates `Prepare report` and another test expects the database to contain no tasks. If the tests share a database without proper cleanup, the second test may fail depending on execution order.

A better approach is to make test data explicit and isolated.

For example, your E2E environment might use a dedicated PostgreSQL database and reset it before a test suite or before individual tests, depending on the required isolation.

You might have a predictable test user such as:

~~~text
email: e2e-user@example.com
password: test-password
~~~

The exact strategy depends on your application, but the principle is simple: **an E2E test should control the data it depends on**.

Do not make tests depend on whatever happens to exist in a developer's local database.

For larger applications, database reset tooling, seed scripts, transactions where appropriate, or isolated test databases can help. Be especially careful not to let automated tests accidentally connect to a production database.

## Traces and screenshots

When an E2E test fails in CI, the most frustrating situation is often: "It failed, but I cannot see what happened."

~~~callout tip Open the trace when CI fails
With `trace: 'on-first-retry'`, a failed run uploads a trace. `npx playwright show-trace trace.zip` replays every step with DOM snapshots, network calls and console logs — usually enough to fix the test without re-running it.
~~~

Playwright can capture useful debugging information such as screenshots and traces.

A screenshot can show the browser state at the time of failure. A trace can provide a much richer record of the test, including actions, pages, network information, and snapshots depending on your configuration.

For example, Playwright projects commonly enable tracing when a test is retried:

~~~ts
use: {
  trace: 'on-first-retry'
}
~~~

This gives you detailed information when a test fails without necessarily recording a full trace for every successful run.

Screenshots can also be useful for visual debugging, especially when an element is missing or a page is in an unexpected state.

## Running Playwright in CI

An E2E test cannot test an application that is not running. In CI, your workflow therefore needs to start the frontend and usually the backend before Playwright starts testing.

A simplified workflow looks like this:

~~~text
Install dependencies
    ↓
Start PostgreSQL/test services
    ↓
Start Spring Boot backend
    ↓
Start Vite frontend
    ↓
Wait for applications to be ready
    ↓
Run Playwright
    ↓
Upload traces/screenshots if needed
~~~

GitHub Actions can run Playwright as part of your pull-request pipeline. Playwright's documentation provides a GitHub Actions setup that installs the required browser dependencies and runs the test suite.

A typical Playwright configuration can also define a `webServer` so Playwright starts the frontend automatically before tests:

~~~ts
export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev -- --host 0.0.0.0',
    url: 'http://127.0.0.1:5173',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
~~~

For a full-stack application, you may need an equivalent strategy for the Spring Boot backend and its database. The important part is that CI creates a predictable environment before running the browser tests.

## Keep the E2E suite small

Because E2E tests are relatively expensive, do not turn every tiny requirement into an E2E test.

Suppose a task form has ten validation rules. You probably do not need ten browser tests. Unit or component tests can cover detailed validation behaviour, while one or two E2E tests can prove that the main workflow works through the complete stack.

A sensible distribution might be:

- unit tests for business rules
- integration tests for database and backend integration
- frontend tests for component behaviour
- a small number of E2E tests for critical user journeys

For the task manager, good E2E candidates include:

- a user can log in
- an authenticated user can create a task
- a user can see their existing tasks
- an important authorization boundary works from the browser

You do not need an E2E test for every CSS class or every internal React state transition.

## Common mistakes

### Using fixed delays

Avoid `waitForTimeout` as a general synchronization strategy. Wait for the condition that matters instead.

### Depending on test order

A test should not require another test to run first. Give each scenario the data it needs and reset the environment appropriately.

### Using fragile selectors

Avoid selectors based heavily on CSS structure or generated class names. Prefer roles, labels, and meaningful accessible names.

### Testing everything through E2E

E2E tests are slower and more expensive than unit and component tests. Keep the suite focused on important user journeys.

### Sharing uncontrolled data

If tests depend on whatever happens to be in the database, they can become flaky. Use predictable test users and controlled test data.

### Ignoring failures in CI

Configure traces, screenshots, and other artifacts so a failed test gives you enough information to investigate what happened.

## The practical goal

An E2E test should feel like a short, automated version of an important manual acceptance test.

For example:

~~~text
"A user can log in and create a task."
~~~

That sentence is already close to an E2E test specification.

Playwright turns it into executable behaviour: navigate to the application, find the login controls, enter credentials, click the button, create the task, and verify that the task is visible.

Use E2E tests where confidence in the complete system is worth the additional cost. Keep them short, use accessible locators, rely on Playwright's auto-waiting, control your test data, and collect useful diagnostics when something fails.

That gives you a small suite of tests that protects the most important paths through your application without turning every frontend change into a slow browser test.
takeaways: E2E tests verify important workflows across the frontend, backend, and database as a user experiences them.
Playwright provides browser automation, accessible locators, assertions, and automatic waiting.
Control test data and reset the database so tests do not depend on previous runs.
Use traces and screenshots to make CI failures easier to investigate.
Keep E2E tests small and focused on critical user journeys because they are more expensive than lower-level tests.

quiz.question: What is the main thing an end-to-end test proves?
options: That every React component has 100% code coverage
That one Java method returns the expected value
That an important user workflow works across the complete application stack
That the application's CSS contains no errors
quiz.explanation: An E2E test exercises the application through the browser and can verify that the frontend, backend, database, and other required parts work together.

quiz.question: Which locator is generally preferable for an input labelled "Title"?
options: page.getByLabel('Title')
page.locator('.input-7f82')
page.locator('div > div:nth-child(3) input')
page.locator('[style="width: 300px"]')
quiz.explanation: getByLabel uses the accessible label and is more closely tied to how users identify form controls.

quiz.question: Why is Playwright auto-waiting useful?
options: It makes the backend respond faster
It waits for expected UI conditions instead of requiring arbitrary fixed delays
It automatically fixes failed tests
It prevents the browser from making network requests
quiz.explanation: Playwright can wait for elements and assertions to reach the expected state, making tests more reliable than fixed sleep-based synchronization.

quiz.question: Why should E2E tests use controlled test data?
options: So tests can depend on the order in which developers run them
So production data can be modified during testing
So the tests become dependent on a shared developer database
So each test has predictable data and is less affected by previous runs
quiz.explanation: Predictable and isolated test data prevents failures caused by leftover records or differences between environments.

quiz.question: Why should an E2E suite usually contain fewer tests than a unit-test suite?
options: E2E tests cannot make assertions
E2E tests are generally slower, more complex, and more expensive to maintain
E2E tests only work on Linux
E2E tests cannot interact with forms
quiz.explanation: Browser-based tests exercise much more of the system, so they cost more to run and maintain. They should therefore focus on important user journeys.

exercise.title: Build an end-to-end testable Add Task flow
exercise.task:
Build a single-page Add Task flow in plain HTML and JavaScript. Create a form containing a real label connected with htmlFor/for to a text input with id="title" and the accessible name "Title", plus a due-date input with type="date" and id="due". Add a submit button named "Add task", a
    with aria-label="Task list", and a

    with role="status" and id="status". When the form is submitted with an empty title, the status must read exactly "Title is required" and the title input must have aria-invalid="true". When a valid title is submitted, add an li reading " (due <date>)" when a date was supplied, or just "<title>" when there is no date. After a successful submission, clear both form fields, reset aria-invalid to "false", and set the status to "Task added". The tests interact with the page like a Playwright test: they locate controls using their accessible labels/roles, fill fields with typeInto, click the submit button, and verify visible text and accessibility attributes.
exercise.starter: Add task
exercise.solution: Add task
exercise.hint: Treat the submit handler like a small user-facing workflow: trim the title first, handle the invalid case by updating both the status text and aria-invalid, then create an li for valid data. Use textContent for the task text. Append the item, call form.reset(), restore aria-invalid to false, and finally show "Task added".

tests.name: It exposes the controls with accessible labels and roles
It reports the validation error for an empty title
It adds a task with a due date and clears the form
It adds a task without a due date
It can recover from validation failure and then submit valid data
